skyline.text: How a crowded street fed a worldwide population panic
Why tyranny makes people stop having children, from Poland to Russia
Five metals, ten years, and a prophecy of doom undone

footnote.text: Human beings are the ultimate resource.

brief.head: Crowded, and rich
brief.text: Monaco is forty times as dense as Bangladesh and far richer, Amit Varma said, citing Nicholas Eberstadt, who found no link between density and poverty. {#monaco}

brief.head: Children as insurance
brief.text: The poor have more children because they see them as resources, Amit Varma said. High child mortality made them insurance, yet the pattern persists as mortality falls. {020-C06}

brief.head: Plague as policy
brief.text: Malthus wrote that instead of recommending cleanliness to the poor, we should court the return of the plague. For him, Amit Varma said, plague meant deliverance. {020-J11}

brief.head: Any family will do

brief.head: Out on a bare branch
brief.text: The Chinese call them “bare branches”: young men who never learn a trade, earn an income or build a family. No government dole, Ajay Shah said, can substitute. {020-C15}

thought.text: Tyranny creates hopelessness. And having a child is an act of hope.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, drawing on Hannah Arendt, on why tyrannies run short of children

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why people are an asset
lead.head: More mouths, more minds
body: As a schoolboy in the era of the “Hum Do Hamare Do” slogan, Amit Varma was taught why India was poor: there were too many people. It sounded intuitive. Only in adulthood did he realise the opposite was true. {020-S01}
“That is a canard that we were fed,” Varma said, and it angers him that most people still believe it.
His answer fits in a phrase: people are brains, not stomachs. More people, he said, mean bigger networks, more positive-sum games and more trades that leave both sides better off.
The proof is where people choose to live. All of human history, Varma said, is migration from sparse villages to dense cities. People move from Bihar to Mumbai, not the other way round. {020-C02}
There is a moral point too: calling population a problem, he argued, means calling other people the problem.
## Doom, postponed

The pessimism is old. In 1798 Thomas Robert Malthus argued that resources grow arithmetically and people exponentially, so starvation must follow. In 1967 Paul Ehrlich’s *The Population Bomb* declared that the battle to feed all of humanity was over.

Hundreds of millions would starve in the 1970s and 1980s, Ehrlich predicted. They did not. Such forecasts project a curve into infinity, Varma said, but “anyone statistically knows that you cannot extrapolate a trend and assume that it will continue forever.” {020-C05}
Ehrlich even bet on rising resource prices, and lost. He is still, Varma noted, a hero of the left, though “he has been wrong about everything in his life”.
## The state and the body

The idea had victims. Reading from Coomi Kapoor’s *The Emergency*, Varma described Sanjay Gandhi’s sterilisation drive: quotas for every district and officer, salaries withheld, and police firing on villagers who resisted.
Even if you think population is a problem, he said, coercive family planning tells citizens that “you do not own your bodies”.

Ajay Shah compared three worlds: modest coercion in India before the Emergency, terrible coercion during it, and China’s one-child policy. The more concentrated the power, he argued, the further a mistaken idea escalates into disaster.
## Fear the bust

Then Shah, whose PhD thesis was on fertility, turned the debate around. The danger, he argued, is not a boom but a bust. Tyranny breeds hopelessness, and people respond by having fewer children. {020-C10}
“Having a child is an act of hope,” he said. Russia, which he estimated has lost about 1.3 million people to the war in Ukraine and to emigration, shows the pattern today.
The US and the UK had generations to adjust to slowly falling fertility. In China and Russia the children vanished suddenly, leaving few young people to care for many old ones.

India, Shah warned, may be heading the same way. Its last census was in 2011, but other sources point to a rapid fall in fertility over 10 to 15 years, as would-be parents face cramped homes, long commutes and poor job prospects. {020-C13}
Varma added an image from a friend’s travels in Bihar: streets of idle young men, waiting for nothing. Without jobs, he said, the demographic dividend becomes a demographic disaster.
The hosts ended with two books written long ago about the present: Shah’s pick, Hannah Arendt’s *The Origins of Totalitarianism*, and Varma’s, Irawati Karve’s *Yuganta*.

second.label: Economists’ letters
second.head: I told you so, by post
second.deck: Julian Simon’s fix for overbooked flights, and Milton Friedman’s gracious concession
body: In December 1976 a young Julian Simon wrote to Milton Friedman about overbooked flights. Passengers would write sealed bids for the least they would accept to take the next flight; the lowest bidders would be paid to wait. {#bid}

Friedman agreed the plan made sense, but would not vouch for it to the Civil Aeronautics Board. If it were that good, he reasoned, airlines would already be doing it. Then an economist, Alfred E. Kahn, took charge of the board, and the airlines adopted it. {020-J09}

In 1979 Simon sent Friedman American Airlines’ glowing report on the scheme. Friedman’s reply was short and gracious, and Amit Varma loved it: great people in dialogue, with no ego involved. {020-S08}

quote.text: Many thanks for your I told you so, you are entitled to it.

second.caption: Julian Simon’s letters to Milton Friedman

third.head: Standing room only
body: Amit Varma’s friend Kumar Anand lives in Saharsa, in Bihar. Travelling through semi-urban Bihar near the town, he saw streets full of young men, standing. {020-S07}

They were not waiting for a bus, Varma said, or smoking at a katta, or waiting for a contractor’s truck to take them to work. “They’re just standing. They’re just idle,” he said. It was a haunting image.
Kumar Anand and Mohit Satyanand later took a road trip through Bihar for Varma’s podcast, *The Seen and the Unseen*. Much of what they found was young people who had no jobs, or no longer cared.
“What kids are you gonna have?” Varma asked. Without jobs, he concluded later, the demographic dividend becomes a demographic disaster. {#dividend}
third.caption: the idle young men of Bihar

p2.title: In defence of people
p2.deck: Amit Varma on a history of population panic, Ajay Shah on why the real danger is a bust {020-C11}

sections.label: The premise
sections.head: Brains, not stomachs
sections.caption: people as brains, not stomachs
body: Amit Varma had wanted to make this case for a long time. He began with a 2007 study, Nicholas Eberstadt’s *Too Many People?*, which found no correlation between population density and poverty. Monaco is forty times as dense as Bangladesh and far richer; Bahrain is three times as dense as India and far richer. {#monaco}

You don’t even need the data, he said, only common sense. If density made people poor, they would flee it. Instead, “the whole story of humanity, all of human history, is about migrating from sparsely populated rural areas to cities with dense populations.” {020-C02}
## The ultimate resource
His motto, people are brains, not stomachs, echoes the economist Julian Simon, whose *The Ultimate Resource* argues that human beings are the ultimate resource. {020-R02}

Simon’s last book, *The Great Breakthrough and Its Cause*, finished by Timur Kuran, goes further: the industrial revolution and productivity booms happened because population rose. More people multiply the chances to trade, and everyone benefits. {#kuran}
Varma then challenged the viewer. If you are watching in a city, why are you there? If you are in a village, he said, either you made your money in a city or you want to go to one.
~ Ask yourself, he said: “Would you say you’re a burden on the planet, or would you say that you’re contributing something to it?”

quote.text: More people mean greater networks, more positive sum games, more double thank you moments.

sections.label: The history
sections.head: Bombs, quotas and bullets
sections.caption: the horrors of population control
body: The idea that people are a burden goes back to 1798, when Thomas Robert Malthus argued that resources grow arithmetically while people grow exponentially. {020-R05}

Amit Varma traced it through Harrison Brown, who compared humanity to maggots on a dead cow and backed forcible sterilisation, to Paul Ehrlich’s 1967 *The Population Bomb*, which announced that “the battle to feed all of humanity is over.” {020-R06}

The panic became policy worldwide. Charles Mann records health workers paid by the number of IUDs they inserted, and birth-control pills pitched out of helicopters over villages in the Philippines. {020-R07}
## Quotas from the top

In India, Varma read from Coomi Kapoor’s *The Emergency*. Sanjay Gandhi bypassed the nodal ministry and went straight to chief ministers eager to please him. Sterilisations rose from 26.24 lakh in 1975-76 to 81.32 lakh in 1976-77, and Haryana hit four times its target. {#lakh}
Every district and officer had quotas. Teachers had to “motivate” at least five sterilisations to be paid. Some Delhi government hospitals refused treatment until the patient agreed to be sterilised.
~ Even today, Varma said, incentives are given to doctors across rural India to produce sterilisations, and it is always the women who suffer. {#incentives}

quote.text: Some desperate teachers were so frantic to meet their quotas that they offered half their salaries to persuade volunteers to undergo the operation.
quote.who: Coomi Kapoor, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: The city
sections.head: Twenty minutes from greatness
sections.caption: the greatness of cities
body: Ajay Shah built his intuition from cities. In *Triumph of the City*, Edward Glaeser explains that cities are great because they pack large numbers of clever people close together. {020-R11}

“It’s the number of people that live within 20 minutes of you,” Shah said. {020-C03} Their combined human capital challenges and drives you: we are each creatures of the people around us. Scatter everyone on a grid 100 metres apart, and that flowering dies.
Modern culture, he argued, is urban, made in dense collections of people, not in the landowner’s machismo of rural life.
## Not destiny, but governance
Glaeser also shows that dense cities can be terrible, with crime, slums and troubles of public health. New York in the 1970s, Shah said, was famous for crime, rats and cockroaches.

Amit Varma added a lesson from Bjørn Lomborg’s *The Skeptical Environmentalist*: around the turn of the 19th century, London was as polluted as any Indian city today, and it later grew much cleaner. {020-R12}
Nothing about that arc is inevitable, Shah cautioned: it takes purposeful human action. But public health and urban planning for transport and parks, he said, are solvable problems. {020-C04}
~ Even a Mumbai slum, the hosts agreed, is better than a village: people are voting with their feet.

quote.text: These are not beyond the wit of man, and these are solvable problems.

sections.label: The state
sections.head: No ceiling on coercion
sections.caption: degrees of coercion
body: Ajay Shah compared three worlds of family planning: pre-Emergency India, with modest coercion; Emergency India, subject to the whims of one or two people; and China under the one-child policy, “Draconian beyond belief”. {020-C07}
The lesson, he said, is about concentrated power: when nobody dares tell the dictator he is wrong, terrible ideas take hold. The answer is to disperse power and make such intrusion illegitimate.

A government that tried to stop him having children would be creepy, Shah said: “I have no children today, but that’s my goddamn birthright.” {020-C08} Coercion also comes in degrees. Stopping a Punjab farmer from burning his field is mild; telling a single woman she cannot use surrogacy is “a different level of evil altogether”.
## The missing brake
Spending, Shah argued, has a built-in brake. Taxes are hard to extract: people rebel, move their money abroad, dig holes and hide their wealth. So even a half-witted government weighs what it spends.
Coercion has no such limit. Governments pile one rule on another, with no cap on the total and no fine sense of degree. “There’s no budget constraint in coercion,” he said. {020-C09}
~ Citizens, he concluded, must rebel far more against intrusive coercion. Questions about having children should be “the bloody business of individuals”.

quote.text: Many terrible ideas become accepted because nobody has the guts to tell the dictator that you’re full of it.

sections.label: The bust
sections.head: When the cradles empty
sections.caption: the danger of a population bust
body: Having a child, Ajay Shah argued, is an act of hope. Drawing on Hannah Arendt, he said tyranny breeds hopelessness and stagnation, and men and women respond by going on strike. {020-C10}

Russia shows it today. About 300,000 men of reproductive age have died in Ukraine, he estimated, and about a million of the best and brightest have left, taking a future stream of children with them. {#russia}
## The arithmetic of age
The real danger, then, is not a boom but a bust. The US and UK declined slowly, giving society generations to adjust. In China and Russia, the children vanished suddenly. {020-C11}

Set money aside, Shah said, and look only at people. The old need nursing, cooking and cleaning, which only the young can provide. If ten old people need fifteen young ones, that works. If they need sixty, it cannot, and the price of those services heads towards infinity. {020-C12}

India, he warned, may be next. Other sources point to a rapid fall in fertility, as would-be parents face cramped homes, long commutes, a skewed sex ratio and a rule that young people need a job before marriage, when jobs are scarce. {020-C13}
~ Amit Varma saw a vicious circle: lose hope, have fewer children, grow older, and find still less cause for hope.

quote.text: And far from the fears of a population bomb. Today we understand the damage from a population bust.

side.boxText: Julian Simon’s *The Ultimate Resource*, which Amit Varma said came out in 1981 and has a second edition, argues that human beings are the ultimate resource. Its thesis is the root of the episode’s claim that people are brains, not stomachs. {020-R02}

contQuote.text: Do they see jobs? Do they see freedom? Do they see safety? Or do they see a grim, troubled world where there is social strife, an ever-interfering state, and poor economic prospects?

stories.caption: the siege of Pipli
stories.kicker: Amit Varma reads Coomi Kapoor on a village under siege
stories.head: The night they came for Pipli
body: Pipli is a village in Haryana, 45 kilometres north of Delhi. During the Emergency it became the epicentre of a major riot, Amit Varma said, reading from Coomi Kapoor’s *The Emergency*.
It began with a widower, Hawa Singh, who had been forcibly taken for sterilisation. His incision turned septic, his wound festered, and he bled to death.

The block development officer was unrelenting. He came back demanding more volunteers, and had a man repairing shoes by the roadside picked up. Furious, the villagers drove the officer and his men out after a scuffle.

Retaliation was swift and brutal. Several hundred policemen arrived, ordered the men out of their homes and laid siege to the village through the night. At 6 am shots were fired, and two women making cow-dung cakes outside their huts were mowed down.

A warning followed: if the villagers did not come out, an aircraft would be sent to bomb the whole area. The men surrendered. Out of a population of 2,761, between 400 and 500 were rounded up and sterilised. {#pipli}

For Varma, the deeper horror is the message. Even if you believe population is a problem, he said, the state is telling its citizens that “you do not own your bodies”, which is worse than slavery. And yet it was normalised. {020-S04}
~ Pipli was not alone. Between August and December 1976, Kapoor writes, police opened fire at least eight times on people resisting the drive. In three towns alone, twelve people died. {#firing}
stories.why: Once a policy becomes a number passed down a hierarchy, every link in the chain has a reason to coerce the next. The cruelty came from the design of the incentives, not a few bad apples. {020-S03}
stories.postscript: Kapoor, Varma said, is a great journalist, and she has also been a guest on his podcast *The Seen and the Unseen*.

stories.caption: Paul Ehrlich’s taxi ride
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the Delhi ride behind a population panic
stories.head: Fleas, dust and a doomsday book
body: Paul Ehrlich wrote that he came to understand the population explosion emotionally one stinking hot day in Delhi. {#taxi} In an ancient taxi hopping with fleas, he and his family crawled through a crowded slum in heat well over a hundred degrees.
He saw “people, people, people, people”, and wondered whether they would ever reach their hotel. “And I’m pleased to report he did get to his hotel,” Amit Varma said. {020-J03}

Ehrlich also wrote that he could not see how India could feed 200 million more people by 1980. {#feed} Since that ride, Varma said, Delhi’s population has grown five times, though in the mid-sixties the city was not that crowded. Ehrlich, he said, was “clearly lying”. {020-S02}
~ Such forecasts, Varma said, came from extrapolating figures: at one point Ehrlich imagined 70 billion people visiting each other by elevator, because there would be no roads.
stories.why: The era’s most influential population panic rested on a recoil from crowds of poor people, not on evidence. The city that horrified Ehrlich went on to absorb many times more people. {020-S02}

stories.start: Paul Erlek at one point remarks, if I were a gambler
stories.end: Edley goes on and he's still, as I pointed out, uh a major figure
stories.caption: the Simon–Ehrlich wager
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a bet that put a prophecy to the test
stories.head: Ehrlich bets, Simon collects
body: In the 1970s, Paul Ehrlich remarked that if he were a gambler, he would take even money that England would not exist in the year 2000. {020-S05}

The economist Julian Simon noticed the word “bet” and, very publicly, took him up on it. Ehrlich could choose five resources and any period longer than a year. Simon would wager, Amit Varma thought about $10,000, that their prices would fall.
Ehrlich chose copper, chromium, nickel, tin and tungsten. The bet was made in 1980. By 1990 the prices of all five had fallen, as anyone who knows Econ 101 would expect, Varma said. {#ninety}
~ Yet Ehrlich remains a major figure, his articles still appearing in big newspapers abroad. “Paul Ehrlich, by the way, is a hero of the left even today,” Varma said.
stories.why: Putting money on a prophecy exposes it to reality. Scarcity sets off ingenuity and price adjustment, so resources do not simply run out as people multiply. Being wrong, though, rarely costs a public intellectual his standing.

stories.start: I know some of these things, I have an amusing fact for you
stories.end: bring our children into? Will there be safety? Will there be prosperity?
stories.caption: Poland’s birth strike
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a favourite tale from his PhD reading
stories.head: Between two bad neighbours
body: Ajay Shah had “an amusing fact” to share: his PhD thesis was on fertility, about women in Malaysia having babies, which sent him deep into the fertility literature. {020-S06}
His favourite story from it is Poland. A young country born out of the Treaty of Versailles, it was invaded by the Soviets almost at once, and Leon Trotsky was stopped at its edges.

Then came a precarious life between Germany and the Soviet Union, both, Shah said, terrible neighbours to have. So birth rates collapsed, with no modern reproductive technology. “When hope dies, you stop having children,” Shah said. {#hope}
~ To have children, he said, you need to be in a certain place, in your heart and in your sense of the world: “What kind of world are we going to bring our children into?”
stories.why: Fertility tracks how people see the future. Fear alone, under hostile neighbours or a tyrant, can make a society stop having children, with no pill required. Shah sees the same pattern in Russia today. {#russia}

quiz.q: Which five metals did Paul Ehrlich pick for his wager with Julian Simon?
quiz.a: Copper, chromium, nickel, tin and tungsten, and all five were cheaper by 1990.

quiz.q: According to Nicholas Eberstadt’s study, how does Monaco compare with Bangladesh?
quiz.a: It has forty times the population density, and is far richer.

quiz.q: Why did Thomas Robert Malthus, writing in 1798, think mass starvation was inevitable?
quiz.a: People grow exponentially while resources grow only arithmetically, so resources would run out.

quiz.q: What was the subject of Ajay Shah’s PhD thesis, his “amusing fact”?
quiz.a: Fertility, specifically women in Malaysia having babies, which took him into the literature.

quiz.q: In an ageing society, why do personal services for the elderly become unaffordable?
quiz.a: Only the young can provide them and they can’t be imported, so prices soar.

quiz.q: During the Emergency, what did government teachers have to do to be paid?
quiz.a: Motivate at least five sterilisations; some offered half their salaries to find volunteers.
